Great for home office. Note on power management settings in WIN 10. Great machine. Installed a SSD and 8G ram. Upgraded to Windows 10. There was an initial problem with random screen freezes (requiring a hard restart). After lots of searching and effort my solution was, set the power management settings in windows to 'maximum performance' AND in power options (WIN 10) disable "Selective USB Suspend". Three day into those changes and all is well. That was my experience. It is in use in my home office (accounting software, MS Office etc) mounted to the rear of one monitor. It supports dual monitors nicely (I got a DP to VGA cable adapter).

I purchased a GoPro Hero5 Session under some sort of ... I purchased a GoPro Hero5 Session under some sort of Amazon Promotion - $300 for the camera plus a $45 gift card. For those that don't know, at time of purchase, and writing, the camera itself was $300. The back plate was starting to peel off, and the button would slide under the case. The operation of the product was degrading. I sent the camera in for repair under this warranty that I purchased, and over a week later, this is my resolution. 1) First off, they were relatively quick with responding to my request. 2) About 4 days later I received notification that my repair was approved, but would not be repaired by them, it would be sent back to me, I would have to bring it to a local shop, send in the receipt, and then be reimbursed. 3) The following day, I was told that my item was unrepairable, and that I would be receiving a check to settle the warranty. The check was to be for $255, due to a unique way Amazon broke up the deal, which some might argue is fair, I did not. I looked at my purchase as a $300 GoPro with a free $45 gift card. But whatever. 4) I call up, attempting to get them to reimburse the full price of the purchase, to no avail. Through conversation I find out that by settling the warranty with a payout, the warranty is null and void. 5) I was told the reason I was being paid out was that they did not have any replacements in stock. I told them I'd rather wait until they did have a replacement in stock, as this is the only condition that guarantees continuity of warranty. Was told I could not wait. Spoke with a floor supervisor, was told this gem... They DO NOT carry replacement cameras to send back in the event your item is "unrepairable." Every bit of marketing of this plan indicates repair or replacement is possible, but there is absolutely nothing to indicate that they do not replace cameras. They only replace "low end tablets and phones." I imagine that this is their business practice - claim unrepairable, sell the broken or defective products to their depot to be parted out and sold for a profit. Of course, depending on what makes them the most money. This type of marketing is incredibly misleading. If you are purchasing for a camera, please note: this warranty will very likely be a one and done for you, depending on the camera. I don't even know if they repair anything, considering that it was just a back plate in my camera that needed replacement, and they declined to repair that. For all those claiming peace of mind, I suppose this plan does offer you some comfort and protection, but the very misleading nature of the way Amazon markets this warranty means I will never purchase another.

Dead after just 1.5 months of use I bought this router on July 13, 2016 and until yesterday (August 29,2016) didn't experience any issues. Yesterday evening none of my wired or wireless devices (desktops, tablets, ROKU players to name a few) could connect to the Internet. I thought it was the issue with Time Warner Cable so I started playing with my cable modem (restarting, resetting, etc). Nothing. Then I restarted the router. Nothing again. I performed factory reset. Nothing. Lights are blinking as usual, strong 2.4GHz and 5GHz signals everywhere, the router's config web page at 192.168.1.1 shows that everything is fine including internet access... just no internet connection in real world. Just in case, I decided to connect my laptop directly to the cable modem, and it worked. 35Mbps down and 6Mbps up as expected, which means the router is dead after just 1.5 months of use, and this is unacceptable for a premium product. Of course it's too late to return in to Amazon so I guess I'll have to enjoy ASUS RMA process. I already know that I will have to pay for shipping... thanks God, it's not a freezer ;-)

A Must Buy For the Serious UAV Video Photographer. I highly recommend buying the bundle from this seller for the professional video photographer. It comes with a backpack to carry the Phantom 4, 2 batteries for a full hour of video photography, the remote controller, 8 propellers, and other accessories. The backpack contains many pockets to hold instructions, UAV certificates, etc. I can carry the backpack comfortably while hiking or riding on a bicycle to remote areas. The main reason I purchased from this seller is the saving realized by buying a bundle, instead of buying separate items. I have flown the Phantom 2, the Phantom 3 Advanced, and now the Phantom 4. The latter is really the state of the art from DJI. The DJI GO app works flawlessly this time, unlike the previous experience I had with my Phantom 3 Advanced. Updating the firmware on the Phantom 4 is accomplished much more easily and less complicated too. You download the Phantom Installer into your computer, hook up your quadcopter with the cable provided, and everything is updated automatically. Very user friendly! The Phantom 4 comes with Tap Fly and Collision Avoidance, extra features not found on the Phantom 3 series. These are new "Smart" technology coming from DJI. With these latest "Smart" technologies from DJI, anyone can confidently fly the Phantom 4 in the Washington DC without any incident. I say it because some dumb guy flew his Phantom 1 or Phantom 2 over the White House and crashed his drone over the White House lawn. Excellent work DJI, keep the good work going with new progress!

A Customer Support Story! When I first received these headphones, the right speaker projected constant static that made it unusable. I researched online and couldn't find anyone with the same problem, so I contacted customer support (via email). They got back to me promptly and walked me through some tests, but it quickly became clear it was a hardware issue. They were very nice, and offered me a replacement free of charge. All I had to do was print out a shipping label they provided and send back the pair I had. The new pair arrived and works great! Pairing was just a little bit tricky (I saw 3 things on bluetooth for android, each of the headphones, and also something labeled "Here One"), but once they were paired, the sound was STUNNING! Other people have mentioned features being missing for android, but they're all available for me. You just have to hit bypass, and then there are all sorts of noise canceling settings (like for planes) that work incredibly well. The case is small, the headphones fit great (and stay in even if I'm running or being active). All in all, a wonderful product!

Good quality SSD for fast disk access and reliable performance This SSD drive from Toshiba is one that can boost speed over SATA drives. This drive is very slim and installs smoothly in a typical 2.5" SATA drive slot. The instruction guide comes with explanations for how to set up and format the drive with the operating system you are running. The drive was easy to install and get running, and the file operations run smoothly on the drive. (freedom of speech) It is my belief that to stop the monetary bleeding the following scheme has been implemented: 1) Produce an inferior product subject to early failure. (plenty of evidence to support that reality) 2. Offer a warranty that is very short (realistically 90 days) with major costs passed on to the purchaser after 90 days. 3) Tie this warranty to a long term programming service purchase THAT CANNOT BE TRANSFERRED to a replacement device. 4) Make the "lifetime service" apply to the device rather than the lifetime of the purchaser. It's in the fine print if you have the time and determination to find it. Tivo is banking on most people not spending the time to uncover these conditions that would likely be unacceptable if known. 5) Have Tivo CS agents make claims as difficult as possible to process. Moderately helpful in some cases; not a long range solution. I have a router configured as a bridge in my barn, approximately 120 yards from my home. The router is fairly basic, running DDWRT firmware and using the stock 5dbi antennas. I get a good enough connection, but I was looking for an inexpensive, easy way to improve speeds without running cable or mounting large antennas. I first installed these on my home router. Installation was simple; screw off the old antennas, screw on the new ones. Almost every consumer wireless router or PC card is compatible with RP-SMA connectors. I then headed to the barn to run a few speed tests on multiple sites and compare them to earlier results. I saw no noticeable differences between the two sets of antennas. I then replaced the home router's default antennas and replaced the ones on my barn router, then ran the same tests. Again, no noticeable difference. Of course, 9dbi omnidirectional antennas aren't an ideal solution for this range, but I was still hoping for some improvement. On the plus side, a wireless TV box on the far end of the house does get a moderately improved signal with these antennas, so there is some improvement to be had from these. Disclosure: This product was provided to me at a discount for consumer feedback. All opinions are my own.

ONE OF THE BEST SOUNDING SOUNDBARS OUT THERE.  RICH CLEAR OPEN SOUND FOR VOICE, MOVIES, AND CASUAL MUSIC LISTENING. Very Good Sound. Open, rich, natural, can be played loud, and NOT a little boxed in and lacking in the vocals in like my older Yamaha Sound Bar or even the newer ZVOX SB500 that I had at the same time and did an A-B With. The ZVOX sounded a little thin and tin like and slightly boxy to me compared to the richer more open sound of the Pioneer SP-SB23W. This Pioneer sound bar offers Optional bluetooth for your music, another setting for movies, and another setting for voice. The voice pretty much cuts the subwoofer, the music ads modest bass and subwoofer, and the movie seems to had more to the treble and the bass. The subwoofer is adjustable on all settings. I had a little trouble getting the subwoofer to sync at first. However, even though they originally ask you to push the button on the main soundbar and sub for them to sync originally, if you ever loose the sync with the subwoofer, you can unplug the subwoofer and just push the sync button on it without dealing with the main soundbar button again or maybe even wait and the sub syncs on its own later. By the way, I have a high end stereo system that I assembled over the years which will challenge most stereo systems around, and know good sound when I hear it. Bear in mind, no soundbar with its physical and design limitations will compare to a larger stereo system in quality. The design of the Pioneer is a little mousy and boring looking, but at a distance under the TV it looks fine and more importantly, for a soundbar, what you hear is one of the best soundbars out there. PERIOD. Why not. It has numerous larger drivers instead of tiny ones. The subwoofer is wireless and a little small, but for that reason, integrates better with the sound than some others easily produces rich deep bass (adjustable) for music and videos and being wireless lets you move it to an ideal location. I suspect that bigger is better and the physics of the larger speaker drivers in this sound bar and isolated amplifiers is what delivers the rich sound heard in comparison to other soundbars I have hear. I hear clear yet rich quality dialog and good dynamic response with movies and music. The Pioneer SB-SB23W allows you to use the Bluetooth function to control it with your iPad, phone, computer, etc. So if you have a library of digitized music on your computer or phone or want to use music and radio services to play through it, for its size, it will not disappoint and can fill your livingroom or even most of your house with sound. This soundbar will learn the buttons on your TV remote also. You just hold down the learn button until it flashes or turns solid blue, use the Pioneer remote and touch the key you want to program, then touch your corresponding remote key, they touch the pioneer one last time to program that key and continue through everything on your remote that you want to program, then hold down the learn key again until it stops flashing or turns solid blue which finalizes programming. I mention this because a u tube video by pioneer says to hold down the learn key until it turns a solid blue, and from my experience, a flashing blue is what you really get with my unit to trigger the learning mode. This subwoofer is being clearanced, so I assume a newer more modern one is coming out. However, don't assume it will sound as good or better, especially for the price. The trend is toward slimmer smaller soundbards with smaller speakers that can't match larger drivers in quality and volume of sound. My older Yamaha soundbar did not sound as good, and could not be played loud like this Pioneer sound bar. Bear in mind that CNET in its 2018 review, even with the new soundbars in place, still put this soundbar above most of the slightly more attractive newer more expensive and slimmer units sound wise. If you can get past some of the reliability complaints, this is one of the best sounding soundbars under $1,000 out there. There have been some complaints historically about reliability. Perhaps Pioneer has corrected these problems over time. I have had mine for about a month, and I have no problems. Perhaps buying this Pioneer SB23W at the discounted clearance price brand new and spending the extra $20 for the extended warranty is a very good idea. Another good idea, is to do as I have done and simply to leave it on even if muted at night for about two or three weeks straight. If there are any defects or if anything is going to go out , it will probably do it by then. Either way, know that although it is not the prettiest (nor is it ugly) or quit as fully featured as others , you are buying one of the best sounding sound bars out there for both music and movies at any price.

I'm not going to rip him or his company as these things do happen (they are electronics after all), but the final review will depend on how well this is handled. Addendum: Nick made good on issuing another headphone. This one works. Concerning the phones themselves: I used to play keyboard(s) in a dance band and have been in recording studios (ancient history) so I have some idea as to sound characteristics/issues. When you see technicians in the studio running wires from millions of dollars of equipment to crappy 2 inch speakers you begin to understand that they were in a no win situation for having to satisfy both high-end and low end users. The studios made compromises also and unless you have access to the master tapes you are stuck with their own compromises as to sound. This was true when the medium was vinyl records where the first pass with the needle was the best sound you could get because the grooves that had the higher frequencies were stripped out faster, the tapes that built up oxides and heads that had to be cleaned constantly with tape wear and tear and breakage, to digital CD and flash drives. The weakest part of the chain was always the speaker. It was either too good for the medium or too bad (sometimes because it was too good and would pick up the artifacts). From my perspective, I can see the use of top of the line headphones when editing the master tapes but I have reservations about the effectiveness of using the same when you at the end of the listening chain with all the issues involved with it, from studio to method of transmission and age of recording. All of that affects or degrades the signal. You don't need a Ferrari to go 55 mph on a U.S. highway. Frequency of range is nice for a stat but once you are past being a teenager you start losing the ability to hear the higher end. Pros: the drivers on this thing are massive; phones are fairly light weight; FM is acceptable (actually I'm amending that now-I'm in a fringe reception area and it's pretty good considering-not anywhere as good as my Tivoli, but hardly anything is); excellent battery life. Not Pro or Con: out of the box the bias is toward the bass, but not outrageously so; the genre of music you listen to may determine whether you like it or not. Cons: middle and high-end range is not as balanced with the bass as some would like, and I can't disagree with that; unit itself is somewhat fragile so don't go throwing it at a wall or sit on it; on more sophisticated/complex music tracks there are "separation" issues between various instruments. With all that said these are the best you can get at this price range and are way better than some of the more expensive ones with its drivers. My assumption is that the company took advantage of the massive drivers to deliver the bass to younger listeners and the genres they listen to as they may be the majority buyers. I don't object to the lack of some "tightness" in the sound some have complained about as that compensates to a certain extent for the artifacts that come from weaknesses inherent in Bluetooth and FM transmissions. Sometimes speakers can be "too good" for receiving transmissions. My own tastes are pretty eclectic, running from classical, jazz and country to rock and heavy metal. Despite its weaknesses with some of them I'm fine with how the phones generally operate with these different genres at the price point. If they break I have no problems ordering a new inexpensive one. My take: if an inexpensive speaker setup has to be biased in favor of a set of frequencies I will pick bass. For myself, headphones that are biased toward middle and high ranges are impossible to listen to. I can't stand a "tinny" sound. I have an older Tivoli that has an equalizer that interfaces with its monaural speaker setup on the fly and the sound is impeccable for such a tiny speaker. If this unit were to have anything like that you would easily be in Bose price territory. Here, there is nothing in this price range that sounds as good as these. The five stars were for the performance of the unit at the price point.

I'm pretty sure I read the description of this adapter completely when I bought it ... but re-reading it ... the 2nd to last bullet states that it's not compatible with "low power HDMI ports such as the MacBook Pro with Retina Display". Hmmm wonder if it's been updated in the last week ... Well I can confirm that that is the case and I had to return it for exactly that reason. What happens when plugged into my MacBook Pro is that the Mac recognizes a device is plugged in and switches the display to HDMI and then thinks that the HDMI device was removed switches back ... and then it repeats. From a customer perspective ... Really ... lets put the burden on the user to know if they have a HDMI port which can supply enough current to run Moread's adapter? Oh yes but they listed that MacBook Pro specifically as incompatible ... buried on the 4th bullet ... between a statement that reads like they are compatible with all HDMI ports ("Compatible with PC, laptop, notebook, Apple TV, Roku streaming media player, cable box, and other devices with HDMI port") and "Limited 1-year warranty" ... So how should I rate this device? Lets see ... who is responsible to make sure that the adapter is compatible with the devices HDMI port? A) the user? Short of knowing what your HDMI port can supply and knowing what Moreads adapter draws we can't do it. B) the manufacture of the device with the HDMI port? Does it meet the minimum HDMI spec? If it does they are not to blame. C) Moread engineering to design to the minimum HDMI spec. Hmmm ... this is what engineers are suppose to do ... Are there other devices out there that are engineered to this minimum spec and work ... YES definitely. Hmmm ... guess Moread gets a star maybe two but no more for a poorly engineered device and a marketing group who feels that they can push that poor engineering off on the user ... Even if it does work with someone who has the same PC as you do ... it might not work with yours as HDMI ports are designed to guarantee a minimum spec. The actual current a port can supply varies from unit to unit and over temperature but will always meet that minimum ... so even if it works one day I'd not depend on it working the next. Perfectly suited as a lightweight beater for travel I love this device when I travel. Rather than hauling a 15.6-inch laptop at 5-ish pounds plus a power brick, this T100 is far more sensible. I had faith the Atom processor would ably run Windows 10 based on previous experience with an Intel NUC, and I found that Windows 10 runs all my apps on the T100 with reasonable speed and responsiveness. Whatever penalty in speed there might be, it doesn't register with me, even as I run PowerPoint, Word, and Excel 2010, as well as Citrix Receiver for my remote desktop and VLC for movies. Video calls on Skype work well. I bought the T100 for about $USD160 on sale at the Amazon Warehouse. When I bought the T100, I wanted a lightweight laptop to serve as a "beater" for travelling. My requirements were: cheap, lightweight (about 2 pounds), Windows 10 (I love Android, but I rely on Office and other Windows apps, so a Chromebook seemed like an unnecessary limitation), 64 GB on-board storage (a clean Windows 10 + Office 2010 can be as much as 20-23 GB), minimum 10.1-inch screen, micro-USB charging (no more power brick!), wireless, and a keyboard. The T100 filled these specs, but it should be understood that the T100 is really a tablet with a proprietary detachable keyboard (rather than a fold-over, like a Lenovo Yoga). Wireless has been solid, battery life has been excellent (easily replenished with USB power banks and chargers), and the Windows 10 touchscreen interface is pretty decent (even for taking notes). Bluetooth is also available for when you want to rock a mouse. I had heard good things about the keyboard, and I found it to be very good, although I usually don't preoccupy myself with the keyboard experience. The accessibility tools in Windows 10 are handy when I need to magnify the screen for close work. Should you run out of room on the installed drive, the T100 has an SD card slot for extra room. Ah, but it wasn't always so rosy. Windows 8 was loaded when the T100 arrived, and I fortunately followed advice to download Windows 10 fully before installing rather than doing an online upgrade. Much more of a sure bet that way. Even so, after upgrading to Windows 10, I found a fault in the power switch, so I RMA'd the unit back to Asus for repair/replacement. The unit returned, but with Windows 8, so I upgraded again, then I found another power fault. So I RMA'd >>again<<, this time with Asus paying the freight. Happily, the repaired T100 ran perfectly and has been completely reliable. My hat's off to Asus support for the double-RMA. One more point: the T100 runs 32-bit Windows 10. I have considered upgrading to 64-bit, which should be possible, but on an Atom processor the prospects for improved performance seemed dim, plus I was concerned that there would be no 64-bit driver support. 32-bit has been working fine.

Good for what they are, but be aware that the listing contains much bad information. Updated on 11/18/2016 Apie saw my review and sent a new set with a working power button. Raising to 3 stars. Still good for cutting the grass but their listing says they sound better than Bose or Beats, which is not at all true. For working outside or lifting in a gym, 5 stars. For sound quality and fit, 2.5. As in the title, they are good for what they are, but the Do not compare to the sound of Bose. Updated 09/24/2016 I have used these numerous times over the summer while cutting the grass and can now update my review. In the process I am lowering it from three stars to two. The good news is that the ear cups and electronics have held up well to sweat. That is what I bought it for, despite all my cons, so I'll keep it. That said, there are now more cons. First, after testing them and writing the review I put them away until it was time to cut the grass. When I tries to use them they would not turn on, but when charged showed full. I used them wired that time and planned to send them back. Before boxing them up I tried repeatedly clicking the power button in case there was some corrosion, and they came to life. (Remember, this problem occurred *before* I first exposed them to sweat.) I have now used them at least 8 times, and they will never turn on until I click the button 10-20 times. Second, even with my iPhone 6 in my front pocket or in a case on my arm there are rather frequent dropouts. Not constant, but enough to be annoying and I have tried the phone on both sides of my body. Long story short, these are barely adequate for my purposes in that the ear cups are holding up, but the power switch is poorly made and may not last. ---------------------- I have only had these for a day and will update if things change. Right up front I want to be very clear that I am subtracting two stars immediately for deceptive advertising. In bold letters on the listing title it says these are noise cancelling headphones, but they most certainly are not. Others have said so in many reviews over a long period of time, so I expected that going in, but it bothers me that the sellers haven't corrected the listing. Second, the listing says right at the top that they are "sweatproof", but there is nothing in the manual or on the box to back that up. Finally, below the title in the description it says that in includes a "deluxe carry hard case", but it does not. You get the cheap cloth bag that many have shown in their pictures. So the Amazon listing says two things that are completely untrue (noise cancelling and included hard case) and one that is untrue or at least unsupported by documentation (sweatproof). (Four really, because it calls them "over the ear" when they are really "on the ear", but many people don't understand the difference so I'll give them that one.) To be clear, having read the reviews I understood all of that and ordered them anyway. I need something to wear while cutting the grass, and the ear pieces on my Bose over-the-ear headphones recently self-destructed from the sweat. Replacement pads are on the way, but I wanted something that could survive. Many said they use these for exactly my use-case and they both survived the sweat and blocked sound well, so I'm giving them a shot even if the listing is misleading in many ways. So far so good is all I can say. They paired with my iPhone 6 easily, and sound good enough to this non-audiophile. Some have had problems with the left side not working correctly, but mine are fine so far. Though they are not noise-cancelling they do fit tightly against the ear and do a good job of blocking out outside sounds (making them "noise isolating" rather than "noise cancelling"). Once I have used them for the rest of the season I plan to update this review to say how they deal with sweat. So far I'll say that if not for the very misleading listing I would likely have given them 4 or 5 stars for use while working outdoors.

Overall not too bad but there are a couple things to Think Twice about... I WANT to like this little speaker, I like it's looks...but...it gets 2 stars taken. let me explain. 1st off: The 1st thing I noticed was the clip. The clip isn't even screwed on by both screws that attach the clip to the device. 1 of them fell off/out as soon as I took it out of the packaging. The clip is hard core & stiff.,seems very sturdy & would be more than adequate if it had both screws where they are supposed to be. Not sure how long the clip will last having one 1 screw in place....Due to the clip screw, I take off a star. 2nd: there is branding on the front grill (which I do not mind, it looks cool) that is NOT pictured on the product listing. Not a con, just not expected.. 3rd: The sound quality... I read SEVERAL reviews before making my purchase. They gave this product high marks for it's ability to get loud despite it's small size. Personally, I do not expect much from such a small device as I understand it has limitations. I do not expect super Hi-fi, hence I do not expect boomy bass or really punchy mids...physically it is asking a bit much of physics but there should be at least a small amount of mids just by the properties of the speaker in an enclosure. That said; solid bass is pretty much a no show to the party, the mids are there and do contribute to the over all tone of the device but they lack "luster" due to the overwhelming highs. The highs are SO bright & shrill they destroy what sound quality it might have. I've put a black piece of gorilla tape over the center of the speaker grill to tone down the highs a bit becuz they are so harsh...which has helped unless it is in my pocket or on my hip. In which case using the tape isn't a "need". When turning the device to max volume, it distorts, g it doesn't distort horribly (depending on what you track you are playing) but it does distort as it tries it's hardest to produce bass.. I do want to mention - When you put the device in your pocket the shrill harsh highs drop off & you are left with hearing a more balanced tone & over all sound. No distortion can be heard either. Maybe they took this into account knowing ppl would be putting this in their pockets when designing this device..? Knowing that speakers need a little time to "break in" I am going to give it a day or 2 to see if it relaxes a bit on the treble & the mids start to come through...it might even be able to show signs of bass which might even start to come into play. As for now, the thing sounds like crap & a waste of money. So much so I might even contact Boombotix & see if they will send me a new device...cuz this one sounds terrible. If you double tap the "play/power" button twice it will switch tracks - nice feature. Volume buttons are very responcive, click nice & work very well. 4th: the flap that keeps the USB charging port protected from the elements doesn't really want to stay sealed. It keeps wanting to open. Not cool...BUT what I did end up figuring out is IF you can put the very small round tab in the super small hole located at the tip of the cover (where you open it) it seems to stay in place. I like the look of the device, it has a nice matte finish & seems quite durable overall. Very cool looking packaging presentation & easy to remove with Zero struggling. Pairing is also quick & painless.

Not for anyone with someplace to be. I bought this as a safety measure for when I take the kids hiking I can be sure to always get up back to the car, expecting to at least know the general direction to be heading as the crow flies. I don't think I'm asking too much from this device. It does not perform. I've read all the instructions, I watched all the videos I could find and here is what I found. The compass has to be recalibrate every time you turn it on. It turns itself off after 4 minutes. This might work for you if you can give it constant attention and be sure to push a button within those 4 minutes, but if like me you have little ones to keep an eye on, pass this one by. To calibrate this you have to swing it around in a figure 8 a few times, no less than 5 in my case, then flip it over and over in every possible direction. At this point you are to walk around in a circle. After you have done this have to hold it perfectly level to the ground and turn in until every stop of the arrow continues to point the same way then you should be able trust that it's pointing north and you can now back track to your waypoint, until it turns off again. I just can't do this every time I turn it on. We would never get anywhere. I don't know if mine is defective or if this is how it's suppose to work but it really does not perform as advertised and there is nothing simple about it.

Another cool thing is how easily thes headphones can be stored. Freezing/Hard Lock Hello, I've been having a freezing problem right from the start with this processor on my new Skylake build. I put together this system last month, in January 2016. All parts are brand new and fresh install of windows 10. System: Case: Corsair Carbide Series Air 540 High Airflow ATX Cube Case CPU: i7 6700k Skylake 4.00GHZ GPU: MSI GTX 980 Ti Motherboard: ASUS ROG MAXIMUS VIII HERO SSD: OCZ Storage Vector 180 Series 960GB SSHD: Seagate 4TB PSU: EVGA SuperNOVA GOLD 850W RAM: Corsair Vengeance LPX 32GB (4 x 8GB) DDR4 DRAM 2400MHz OS: Windows 10 64-bit Thermal Paste: Arctic Silver In the off-chance anything might be helpful, and because it's starting to frustrate the crap out of me, here's a dump of everything I've learned so far about my particular issue, and other things that could possibly be related. Alright, so I am experiencing complete system freezes at random moments. Screen remains displaying the moment of the freeze. Also, speakers will occasionally play a harsh deafening sound. Basically, the speakers remain outputting the last tone of whatever was being played at the moment of the freeze, if there was one. The louder the volume is turned up and depending on what tone is being played, it can be very unpleasant and almost deafening if using a headset. With that being said, if the speakers were silent of the time of crash, there will be no "screech of death" since no tone is being played. At first I thought it was an issue with the GPU, sound card, motherboard, etc. Issues pointed towards my audio drivers conflicting. After disabling all audio devices except the speakers and updating drivers the problem still occurs. Problem occurs using both headset and speakers. After a ton of research and troubleshooting I have finally narrowed it down to the new skylake CPU's. I am trying everything to make my PC stable and the longest I've gone without a freeze is 24 hours, maybe 2 days. Sometimes I will get 3-4 crashes in a day if I'm playing a lot. So here is what I've tried so far: Updating various drivers/BIOS. No effect even with the most recent BIOS dated January 7th, 2016. I have also tested the memory using memtest86 returning no errors.. Problem has been reproduced on many storage devices. SSD, SSHD, and HDD. One user even reported freezes during USB flash drive boot-ups. The problem has been reproduced using many different Mobo and RAM manufactures. I personally have tested both corsair and G.skill. Others have reported using crucial, gskill, and corsair with different sizes, frequencies, and mobos. Everyone is getting the same freezes. I am close to RMA'ing just to mess around with some different hardware but I honestly don't think it will fix the issue since others have already tried that. Also, Corsair and G.skill is some of the best memory on the market so I really don't think that memory is to blame here. This has also been brushed off as an overheating issue by some users. I suspected it was overheating since I was crashing at around 70 Celsius while playing taxing games like Ark:Survival on max settings. That's what you do when you build a new rig, right? Then I tested it playing Heroes of the Storm and other low end games. Problem persists even at 40-50 degrees Celsius.. So it can't possibly be an overheating issue. Others have showed similar low temps while freezing occurs. I have also already noted that some users are freezing while idle. Lately I keep Speccy up 24/7 just to see what my temps are during freezes. Temperatures do not seem to correlate with the freezing. So I already mentioned I was able to reproduce the crashing in many different applications, mostly video games like Heroes of the Storm, League of Legends, Smite etc just to ensure it wasn't a problem with any one application. I have yet to freeze during idle, however my system sleeps after 30 minutes so that is probably why I haven't experienced a freeze yet while idling. I am going to turn off sleep mode tonight just to see if I crash while idling. I have ran prime95 tests and pushed my CPU to 100% many times without returning any errors. Also, freezing occurs while playing the most taxing games such as Ark:Survival as well as low end video games such as League of Legends. I've reinstalled windows 10 as a fresh install even though this was a new build and it was already a new partition. Freezing still occurs. Also worth noting that it tends to happen at the most crucial moments of the game(hehe). I have read many posts of people blaming it on a bad batch of CPU's. After doing a ton of research I have found the issue to persist in about 75% of the new Skylake processors. Some enthusiasts have already RMA'd their CPU's two, three, some even 50 times over again with the crashing still occurring. One user made a very strong point worth noting: A big clue is that this is hard locks (not a software lock). You know this because interrupts have stopped.. the system is dead in an unnatural way actually. These are caused by very specific things (usually a race condition of some sort) and usually at a very low level (not software controlled in any way). Yes it can be a failed setup of hardware (bad driver register settings) but its not a software code execution failure, there was no line of code that died in this moment. This points directly to faulty hardware, not a software or driver issue, however it is worth mentioning that a BIOS update may fix it in the future. This is all speculation and doesn't really point towards a fix. However, If I am right, you should all wait a bit longer before RMA'ing since you will not get "fixed" versions until the next gen is released. The most frustrating part of this issue is that it can occur anywhere from 30 mins to 12 hours into a session. It is just really random and almost rare enough for me to just ignore. Extremely unpredictable. However, spending so much money on a new Skylake build I expect flawless performance. Hopefully we can get this issue resolved. I really don't feel like RMA'ing any more parts or downgrading to 5th gen. To anyone with the same issue, please let me know if you find a fix. I will update with any new information. Good luck. Update: Some are blaming bad batch of CPU's. Here is my batch: #L539B636 Also, it passed in Intel Processor Diagnostic Tool Update2: After about a month of troubleshooting I've finally got a stable system. Not even sure what fixed it honestly because I've tried so many solutions. I recently overclocked the CPU and raised the voltages of my RAM in BIOS so I'm pretty sure that's what fixed the crashes. I will update if I crash/freeze again but so far it's been a week with no issues so I think we are good. update3: Started Crashing again after playing some Ark and Black Desert Online this week. I crash about once or twice a day. I play for about 8 hours a day. This really needs to get fixed. I think I am done tinkering with RAM voltages and all this BIOS crap I'm just going to load default and possibly purchase a new CPU. Update4: I finally gave up and ordered a new processor. I down graded to i7 5820 haswell. I'm about 3 months in with no crashes or freezing so the issue was definitely the processor. I'm a little disappointed but at least now my system is stable.

Kickstarter unit never delivered what was promised. Original kickstarter backer here. Some things you should know about Lima before purchasing any of them: Lima is based on the Bifferboard, a 486SX-based computer that was sold as a dev board several years ago. It's basically a 486SX core with some RAM and Flash and some I/O ports. The cheap network drives from 10 years ago used this same core. That's not saying they were bad, as the devices worked well enough (I still have an Eagle-branded unit sitting on a rack, happily cheeping away) but by the time Lima was introduced this silicon was long in the tooth and SLOW. Lima is essentially an Addonics NAS unit, and the original Kickstarter promo photos showed this. These devices sold for around $50, and were essentially a drive-housing-less version of those same cheap network drives I mentioned earlier. Lima promised a lot of things in the original campaign, indicating that they just needed funds to push the unit the last mile and get it manufactured. That turned out to be untrue, as many changes were made along the way and some of the features that were promised during the campaign (external shares, etc.) still are incomplete. Lima may be a "private" cloud device, but you're still required to create an account with Lima's servers. While it doesn't appear that all of your data goes through their servers, they are most certainly seeing metadata of some sort. Be aware of the security risks before trusting Lima to anything that may be important, and remember that Lima promised a third-party code audit that's never happened. During the campaign: Lima tells us that the python codebase won't scale, so they are re-writing it. That makes no sense, as a personal device doesn't need to scale. Turns out that was not really the truth, as the initial installer packages were all written in python. Lima decides to change the housing from the original shown in the kickstarter to something more "flat," in the process removing the power and activity LEDs that are on the original Addonics NAS/Bifferboard the unit is based upon. Lima tells us they need to change some internal hardware and need to qualify it. There's no explanation given. When I finally got my unit: I get a Black and Blue Lima in my hands. The first thing I notice is that there are a number of .py files flying by from the installer, so the noise about re-writing the code was obviously untrue. I have to create an account with Lima, and they suggest using uPnP on my router...why do I need to do this, as it's a "private" cloud? Creating an account and letting an unknown device open ports to the world seems to be going the wrong direction to me. I create the account but refuse the uPnP portion. It comes online, I notice it hard-codes an L: drive on my machine. Thankfully, I don't have a network share on that drive... Putting files onto the unit is extremely slow, and I notice that whatever file I place on Lima is also duplicated on my C: drive! (I'm was told this would change in the future.) The data is stored in a proprietary database, and, while it seems to work well enough, is slower than a glacier and has eaten up the 100GB or so I've dedicated to the OS on my machine. Note, however, that it's speed exactly matches that of the older Bifferboard based units I have, so it's working exactly as fast as the silicon will allow it. (I'm using a 128GB flash drive for Lima, as I didn't have an external rotating platter drive at the time. Turns out Lima doesn't recommend a flash drive, and watching the activity indicator on the drive, I can see why. It's constantly being accessed - if those are writes, then the drive is going to wear quickly. You'll only know not to use a flash drive if you read through some forum somewhere, although I'm hoping they've made this more accessible by now.) A new software update comes along. I have to create a new account...what? I do so, it doesn't work any better than before. A new software update comes along. I have to create a new account...what? I decide that it's not worth the time and consider my money to be lost. Lima only tells me that I need to create yet another account to change the drive and proceed with the new software version. That's another piece of WTF. I have to go through Lima in order to change the drive, and they don't have an easy way of transferring the database from one to another. Sure, you can copy stuff, but it doesn't seem like it's a guaranteed fit. I decided to try and re-purpose the unit. Doing so, I erased the bootloader parameters and made the device useless. Lima's stance on hacking their baby is "YOU NO OPEN!" so they were understandably silent when I asked for the bootloader parameters to repair the unit. That's my fault, and I don't blame Lima for that. I only mention this so if you do decided to break into your unit, don't expect any help, however minimal, from Lima. In all, at the time, Lima didn't do anything near what was promised - it essentially was a poorly designed, slow, unstable network drive with a dirty software load, hard-coded parameters, and accounts tied to an unknown remote service. It didn't (and still doesn't from what I see) work any better than a more professional solution such as a Synology unit. Even if I hadn't killed the bootloader with my incompetence, it still would have eventually wound up in the recycle bin. Don't waste your time or money. Spend it on something that works.

I ended up buying a set of Comply foam tips for these with the hope that they would help it stay in my ear. The Comply tips mostly do work in this regard, but it is another $15 added to the cost. Also, the Comply tips didn't go on easily and wear out after a couple months so the cost will go up. I've never had to purchase replacement ear tips for headsets I've bought before. Actually, out of dozens of BT headsets, I've only had one other one that wouldn't stay in my ears... the original Jaybird Bluebirds X. These Ankers have the same problem. 3. The magnetic function - these have a magnet in them which is supposed to hold the 2 ear pieces together. For example, you could wear them around your neck and magnetically attach them at the front when you aren't wearing them. In practice, the magnet is so weak that it barely works. The magnet needs to be made stronger or should be removed. On the positive side: 1. Battery life is good for earbuds of this size. 8 hours is on the high side for this type of device. 2. The cord is just about the perfect length... not too long and not too short. In all fairness, I did not contact Anker prior to posting this review, because the device isn't broken and my return window with Amazon passed before I really got a chance to try these out (which is my fault). At the end of the day, when adding in the cost of the Comply tips I'm pretty sure I could have gotten a much better set of earbuds for the same price that would have fit better. Very high quality keyboard with nice features and clicky-tactile feel I am a big fan of the classic clicky-tactile keyboards such as those found on the old IBM PC keyboards. My main computer at home still has a Unicomp "buckling spring" keyboard, which is my favorite to type on, but unacceptable if other people are around (those key switches are too noisy for crowded office environments). At my work office, I hated the feel of the generic rubber dome keyboards of the sort that come with practically every computer. I bought a Matias Quiet Pro keyboard, which had the tactile feel and excellent response, but was quiet enough to avoid complaints from coworkers. But the key switches used by Matias seem to have a high failure rate, and I had the first keyboard replaced under warranty, then the second one started to have increasing problems with switches that would not reliable register when pressed, or which would double or triple register when pressed once. Matias seemed unconcerned and actually told me on the phone that these keyboard could only be expected to last about one year! So I dropped the Matias keyboard and looked for a high quality keyboard with mechanical key switches yet a fairly quiet sound level. I settled on this "Das Keyboard 4 Professional Soft Tactile MX Brown" keyboard. It uses the Cherry brand MX Brown series key switches, which are the quieter of the two MX models that have the clicky tactile feel and response ('brown' is the designator of this switch version, and the key switch top and stem are colored brown). At the advice of Das Keyboard (a company in Texas), I also ordered an additional quieting kit from Mechanicalkeyboards.com, which consisted of a bag of clear/white rubber O-rings and a key cap pulling tool. I inserted the O-rings under every key cap, and this cuts the noise of a keystroke by perhaps half, making the overall keyboard even quieter. It is still noisier than the typical generic rubber dome computer keyboard, but it is within reason. This is a very expensive keyboard, so there needs to be performance and physical quality. This is a heavy and solid keyboard, and feels like it is glued down to the desktop when I try to pick it up. The top plate is a heavy thick metal plate with a frosted/matte black anodized finish. The key caps have white lettering, which Das Keyboards says are laser etched; so they are not decals like the cheap keyboards use, and there should be no problem with key cap lettering wearing off. All of the wider keys have mechanical 'bails' underneath, so no matter where you press the kay cap, if moves down smoothly as if you had pressed it dead center. The keyboard also has a very nice 'media center' control panel at it upper right. One key puts the computer to sleep if you press it for a few seconds. Another key toggles sound 'mute' on and off. Three keys act for return-to-start (of a sound file or other sound media), go to end of file, and play/pause toggle. A large volume control knob can be turned from the top or 'rubbed' along its right edge. The keyboard connected to the computer over a USB cable, and the keyboard has two USB pass-through ports on its rear edge just behind the Das Keyboard logo (near the media controls). My one real complaint is that instead of using the traditional legs to tip the rear of the keyboard up to a higher level, this keyboard has a red plastic bar that attaches to the bottom rear of the keyboard using magnets. This just seems kind of dumb, and not an advantage over the conventional way of doing it. Worse, the keyboard actually seems to tilt backwards slightly when the bar is not installed, and is only flat when the bar is installed. To raise the rear for a slight forward slope, as most people are probably used to, you need to put a couple shims of some sort under that bar to make it taller.
